raw_segments.text: One, he said, of which I could not expect easily to convince others.
For let me tell you, Socrates, that when a man thinks himself to be near death, fears
and cares enter into his mind which he never had before.
The tales of a world below and the punishment which is exacted there of deeds done here
were once a laughing matter to him.
But now, he is tormented with the thought that they may be true.
Either from the weakness of age, or because he is now drawing nearer to that other place,
he has a clearer view of these things.
Suspicions and alarms crowd thickly upon him, and he begins to reflect and consider what
wrongs he has done to others.
And when he finds that the sum of his transgressions is great, he will many a time like a child
start up in his sleep for fear, and he is filled with dark forebodings.
